Signal vs Noise: Product vs Measurement

Before you explain why a metric moved, you have to rule out that it never moved at all — it was only measured differently. The discipline of asking "did the product change, or did the tracking?" first.

At 9:40 on the morning of 11 March 2025, Priyansh Sondhi opened the retention dashboard for Balukaa, a quick-commerce grocery app operating out of Jodhpur and expanding into Jaipur and Udaipur, and found that Day-7 retention for new users had fallen from 34% to 19% overnight. Sondhi was three months into the role of Head of Product Analytics, reporting to a CEO, Rhea Ahluwalia, who had just told the board that Balukaa's retention curve was the company's strongest argument for a Series B at a valuation north of ₹900 crore, with the board meeting nine days away. If the fifteen-point drop was real — if the product had genuinely become worse at keeping people — something had broken in the app's core loop: perhaps the 11-minute delivery promise had slipped, perhaps a new onboarding flow confused first-time users, perhaps a competitor's price cut in Jodhpur had pulled customers away. Any of those was a five-alarm problem worth pausing the fundraise to fix. But Sondhi knew a second, more boring possibility was every bit as likely: nothing about the product had changed at all, and the number was lying, because someone had touched the way it was measured. Two things had happened in the same 48-hour window. Engineering had shipped app version 4.3 on 9 March, including a migration to a new push-notification and analytics SDK. A marketing vendor had also updated UTM-tagging rules for paid Instagram campaigns on 10 March. Either, alone, could make a healthy product look like it was collapsing. Sondhi's task for the next two days was not to explain the drop. It was to first find out whether there was anything to explain.

The idea

The distinction Sondhi needed is not a statistical technique so much as a habit of mind, and it has a name in product analytics: signal versus noise, applied to whether an observed change in a metric reflects the product (a real shift in what users are doing) or the measurement (a change in how, or how completely, that behaviour is being recorded). A signal is a metric movement caused by a real change in user behaviour or the product experience. Noise, in this narrower sense, is any movement caused by something other than user behaviour: a broken event, a shifted definition, a new SDK that drops 30% of events on older Android phones, a timezone bug that double-counts an hour, a redefinition of "active user" buried in a pull request nobody flagged as a metrics change. The idea did not emerge from a single paper or inventor; it crystallised through the 2010s as web and mobile analytics matured from simple page-view counters into event-based instrumentation layered across dozens of SDKs and app versions, each capable of silently breaking the pipeline behind the dashboard number. Growth and analytics teams at large consumer platforms formalised this into a discipline sometimes called "metric triage," whose founding move is always the same: before asking why the metric changed, ask whether it changed for real. The problem this solves is expensive. Dashboards present every number with the same visual confidence — a line is a line, a red arrow is a red arrow — regardless of whether it reflects the world or a broken pipe. Without interrogating the pipe first, organisations spend enormous effort solving product problems that were never there, or ignore instrumentation bugs quietly corrupting every downstream decision. The sentence Sondhi could say in Rhea's board-prep meeting without sounding glib was this: "Before we diagnose why retention fell, we have to establish that retention actually fell — two things changed in our measurement pipeline in the same window, and either could produce this exact chart with zero real users behaving any differently."

How it actually works

The mechanics are procedural, and the steps experienced analysts take without thinking are precisely the ones a beginner skips. First, timestamp the suspects: list every change to the product, the instrumentation, the marketing mix and the data pipeline in the window around the metric shift, with exact dates, not vague recollections. Sondhi built this list from three sources — the engineering release log, the analytics team's SDK-and-schema changelog, and the marketing campaign calendar — and this is where most organisations fall down, because the three logs are rarely in one place or cross-referenced against the dashboard. Second, segment the metric by the suspects rather than staring at the aggregate. If version 4.3 is a suspect, split Day-7 retention by app version: did it fall only among 4.3 users, or across the board? This single move is what Sondhi calls "the one that solves 80% of these cases," because a genuine product problem tends to show up everywhere, while a measurement problem shows up exactly and only where the measurement changed. Third, and often skipped, audit the raw event counts feeding the metric, not just the ratio: if the numerator event silently under-fires because of an SDK bug, the ratio moves though nobody's behaviour changed, and the tell is a cliff at a specific timestamp rather than the gradual drift real behavioural change usually shows. Fourth, check a parallel, independently-instrumented metric that should move too if the cause is real — if retention is falling because delivery slipped, complaint tickets or app-store ratings should move as well; if they don't, that is strong evidence the retention number itself is the broken instrument. Finally, reproduce or reverse the suspected change where possible — roll the SDK back for a slice of users, or fire a test event through the new pipeline and confirm it lands in the warehouse — because segmentation and correlation are suggestive, but a controlled reversal is close to proof.

A worked example

Sondhi's cohort was new users who first opened Balukaa between 1 and 3 March 2025, a group of 8,400, of whom 2,856 had returned on day 7, giving the headline 34.0% Day-7 retention the board deck had used for months. The apparent post-shift number, for the cohort turning day-7 on 10–11 March, was 19.2%: 1,612 of 8,400. Sondhi's first move was to split both cohorts by app version. Among users still on 4.2 (who had not auto-updated), Day-7 retention was 33.6% — indistinguishable from baseline. Among users on the new 4.3, it read as 8.9%. That gap was already close to disqualifying "the product got worse," since both cohorts shared the same app, warehouse, delivery network and prices; the only difference was which binary was on their phone. The second move was to check raw event counts rather than the ratio. The "app_open" event day-7 retention depends on had fired 2,856 times for the 4.2 cohort's window but only 402 times for a comparable 4.3 cohort, against an expected ~2,822 if behaviour were unchanged — a cliff, not a drift, and cliffs are the signature of a broken pipe, not 8,000 shoppers changing their minds overnight. The mechanism: the new SDK batched events locally and flushed them only when the app was foregrounded for more than four seconds, a change from the old SDK's near-immediate flush; on the aggressive battery-saving Android devices common among Balukaa's Tier-2 Rajasthan users (roughly 60% of the base), the OS often killed the app before the flush occurred, so real opens happened but were never recorded. The second pass, cross-referencing server-side order logs — independent of the client SDK, and firing only on a real transaction — showed repeat-order rate among the 4.3 cohort at day 7 was 31.9%, only slightly below 4.2's 33.6%, well within what a few genuine early bugs would explain. The defensible statement Sondhi brought to Rhea: real Day-7 retention had likely dipped one to two points from minor 4.3 bugs, not fifteen; the great majority of the apparent drop was the SDK's flush bug undercounting opens on Android.

The nuances a learner must become aware of

Signal-vs-noise is not the same as statistical significance

A newcomer often collapses this into "run a significance test and see if the change is real." A significance test tells you whether an observed difference is larger than ordinary sampling variation, assuming the measurement process itself is trustworthy; it says nothing about whether that process is trustworthy. A metric can move by a statistically airtight fifteen points and still be entirely an artefact of a broken SDK. Significance testing answers "could this be chance?" Signal-vs-noise triage answers a prior question: "is this number even measuring what I think it's measuring?"

The base rate of instrumentation breakage is higher than people assume

Experienced analysts develop a strong prior, earned the hard way, that a sudden, large, single-day step-change is more likely a measurement artefact than a behavioural one. Real user behaviour, in aggregate, tends to move gradually — a slow drift, a seasonal curve, a gentle erosion after a bad review cycle. A metric that falls off a cliff between one calendar day and the next, with no proportional change either side, should raise the prior on "something in the pipe broke" well above half before any investigation begins.

Correlation with a release date is suggestive, never sufficient

It is tempting to see a metric move the same day a release shipped and stop there. But release days also carry confounds — a marketing campaign the same week, a competitor announcement, a holiday shifting the user mix. The discipline is to segment by the suspected cause, as in the worked example, rather than note the coincidence of timing, because segmentation can falsify a hypothesis in a way a shared date cannot.

Not every measurement problem is a bug; some are silent redefinitions

Noise is not limited to broken pipes. A colleague quietly changing "active user" from a 24-hour to a 48-hour window, a data engineer deduplicating events differently after a warehouse migration, a marketing team updating what counts as an "install" — none are bugs in the technical sense, but all produce the same symptom: a metric moving for reasons unrelated to the product. The fix is the same discipline, extended to definitions and pipelines, not only code.

The technique cannot tell you the metric is right, only that it changed for real

Ruling out measurement as the cause of a shift is necessary but not sufficient for trusting the number. A metric can be chronically wrong — systematically over- or under-counting in a stable way — and pass every one of these diagnostics, because they are built to catch changes in the pipeline, not standing biases present from day one. A retention number depressed by ten points because "new user" wrongly includes bot traffic looks perfectly stable under this triage; nothing changed, it was simply wrong all along.

Small teams and single-source metrics are the most exposed

The parallel-signal cross-check that saved Sondhi — client events against server-side order logs — is only available where the same behaviour is instrumented through more than one independent path. A team relying on a single SDK for a critical metric has no independent witness when that source misbehaves, and should treat this as a standing risk to fix before the next release, not a fact to work around mid-incident.

Speed matters more than most teams budget for

Because "the product broke" is more emotionally available than "the pipe broke," teams under pressure often root-cause the product first and lose a day before anyone checks instrumentation. The cheapest defence is procedural: make "what shipped to the product, SDKs, or tracking definitions in the last 72 hours" the mandatory first question on every anomaly alert.

Confidence should scale with how independently the check was made

Before accepting any explanation of a metric move, ask: was it confirmed by segmenting the raw data along the suspected cause, corroborated by an independently instrumented metric, and could the change be reproduced or reversed to test the hypothesis directly? An explanation resting only on "the timing lines up" deserves far less confidence than one clearing all three bars.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

In a high-frequency consumer product like Balukaa, the problem is dominated by mobile SDKs and device fragmentation: millions of events flow daily through client-side instrumentation on a long tail of Android hardware, so any change to that code has an outsized, immediate blast radius. In B2B SaaS, event volumes per account are lower, so one large customer's usage pattern — a procurement team running a quarterly audit — can itself masquerade as a metric shift, and instrumentation changes are more often a backend schema migration than a mobile SDK, with the tell being a step-change aligned to a deploy timestamp in the application's own logs. A B2B analytics lead at Registan Cloud, selling inventory software to Rajasthan's textile exporters, would look first at whether a webhook integration silently changed how "active seat" was counted, since B2B products often redefine usage metrics as they add modules. In a marketplace, a metric can move because of either side of the transaction — Marusthal Bazaar, connecting artisans to retail buyers, could see order-completion fall because buyer behaviour changed, seller listings changed, or the matching pipeline was altered, so the suspect list must cover both sides. The difference by stage is largely about the maturity of parallel-signal infrastructure: an early-stage company usually has one source of truth for any metric and must build the "raise the prior on measurement" instinct deliberately; a large, mature company has redundant instrumentation almost by accident of scale, but pays for it with more places the numbers can quietly disagree, and needs an explicit reconciliation process, not tribal knowledge.

Common mistakes

Mistake one: treating every metric drop as a product post-mortem from minute one. The symptom is a war-room debating onboarding-flow hypotheses before anyone has pulled the release log. The underlying misunderstanding is assuming the dashboard is a faithful witness rather than an instrument that can itself fail. The cheapest diagnostic: a two-minute check of what shipped to the app, the SDKs, or the tracking definitions in the last 72 hours, cross-referenced against the exact timestamp the metric moved.

Mistake two: trusting an aggregate number without segmenting it. The symptom is a team debating "why did retention fall" for days without splitting the metric by app version, platform, or cohort. The underlying misunderstanding is not recognising that a measurement artefact usually has a narrow footprint while a real product problem spreads broadly. The cheapest diagnostic: segment along every suspected cause before forming any causal hypothesis.

Mistake three: mistaking a coincidence in timing for proof of cause. The symptom is a postmortem reading "retention fell the same week we shipped 4.3, so 4.3 broke retention," stated as settled fact. The underlying misunderstanding is confusing correlation in time with a demonstrated mechanism. The cheapest diagnostic: check whether a parallel, independently sourced metric moved in the same direction and by a proportionate amount.

Mistake four: declaring the incident closed the moment a plausible story is found. The symptom is a team that stops investigating as soon as any explanation, however unverified, is comfortable enough for a board update. The underlying misunderstanding is treating plausibility as verification. The cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the explanation has been tested by reproducing or reversing the suspected cause, not merely narrated.

What good looks like

At a comparable company, Thal Mobility, a two-wheeler ride and delivery platform based in Bikaner, a similar Day-7 retention drop appeared three weeks after Balukaa's incident, following a routing-engine update. The analytics lead there, unprompted, opened an incident channel with one pinned message: "Retention fell 9 points starting 2 April. Before we discuss why: what shipped to the app, the routing SDK, or our event schema between 1 and 2 April? Segmenting now." Within ninety minutes the team had split the metric by city, app version and driver-partner cohort, and found the drop isolated entirely to riders on the newest Android build in one city, where a permissions dialog introduced by an OS update was silently blocking the location events the "trip completed" signal depended on. No product hypothesis was floated in the channel; no one speculated about driver quality or pricing. The team fixed the permissions handling, backfilled the missing events from GPS logs held independently by the routing engine, and closed the incident within a day: "Retention did not fall. An Android permissions change under-recorded trip completions for 6% of riders. True retention is flat quarter over quarter." That is the target: instrumentation checked before hypotheses are floated, segmentation done before conclusions are drawn, and a story boring precisely because it is true.

Closing

Sondhi took the recomputed numbers to Rhea two days before the board meeting: true Day-7 retention had likely dipped one to two points from minor bugs in version 4.3, not the fifteen points the dashboard showed, and the dominant cause was a battery-saver interaction with the new SDK's event-flushing behaviour on mid-range Android devices. The board deck was rewritten around the honest number, engineering shipped a hotfix flushing events immediately on app backgrounding, and the dashboard recovered to 32% within a week, closely matching the server-side order data that had been telling the truth throughout. What Sondhi took away, and asked his own analysts to internalise, is that interrogating the pipe before the product is not scepticism for its own sake; it is simply cheaper to check the wiring first than to redesign a working product to fix a symptom the wiring invented. The next thing worth learning, precisely because it depends on getting this right, is anomaly detection and alerting: once a team can reliably tell signal from noise on one incident, the harder problem is building systems that make that judgement fast and consistent every time a metric moves, without rebuilding the diagnosis from scratch each week. Two questions worth sitting with: when your own team last debated why a metric moved, did anyone ask, in the first five minutes, what had shipped to the tracking itself? And what would it cost your organisation, in trust and in decisions already made, if the answer turned out to be "we don't actually know"?

Signal, Noise, and the Instrument

Every number a product organisation argues about is the output of an instrument. This page is about what experienced practitioners do when the instrument and the thing it measures change in the same week — and about the parts of that problem the field has not settled.

1. Two decisions, twelve days apart

On the morning of 6 August 2025, Meher Kaul, VP of Data and Analytics at Kohra Intelligence, a Bengaluru company selling an AI claims-adjudication co-pilot to four Indian health insurers, was looking at a chart she had spent a year earning the credibility to show. Kohra's headline quality metric — the share of extracted claim summaries scored acceptable by an automated evaluator — had risen from 71.4% to 82.1% in one weekly cohort, following the 4 August release of a reworked retrieval step. Kohra's CEO, Vivek Nambiar, wanted the number in the quarterly business review on 19 August and in a renewal conversation with the company's largest insurer, where a contractual quality floor of 80% had been the sticking point for two quarters. Kaul's difficulty was that the same release had also upgraded the evaluator model itself, from a small judge to a larger one, because the small judge had been scoring multi-page discharge summaries obviously wrongly. The product had changed. The instrument had changed. The number had moved eleven points, and nobody could say how much belonged to which.

Twelve days later and 600 kilometres away, Ashutosh Pandhare, head of product at Purvai Energy Networks, faced the mirror image. Purvai sold rooftop solar systems with connected inverters and a monitoring app across Gujarat and Maharashtra; 68,400 systems were live. Its fleet-wide specific yield — energy per kilowatt installed, the number in customer performance guarantees, channel-partner payouts and the monthly pack sent to the lender financing Purvai's receivables — had fallen from 4.32 to 3.91 kWh/kWp, down 9.5%, over the three weeks to 18 August. A commercial customer in Vadodara had filed for an SLA credit, and CFO Leela Iyengar wanted to know by month-end whether this was a bad batch of inverters, a cloudier monsoon, or nothing at all. The window coincided exactly with the staged rollout of firmware 2.9, which had changed how daily energy was computed on the device.

Neither had a measurement problem in the narrow sense of a broken event. Both had the harder version: one release that changed the product and the measurement at the same moment, with a consequential decision sitting on the difference. The competent response is to check whether the tracking changed. The expert response is to assume it did, and then to do arithmetic that assigns the movement between the two with a defensible residual.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

State the distinction precisely. Any reported metric is a composition: a behaviour, a capture process that records some fraction of it, transport and storage that deliver some fraction of that, and a definition that turns records into a number. Write an observed count as O = T × c, with T the true count and c the end-to-end capture rate. Signal is movement in T; noise, in this topic's sense, is movement in c or in the definition — and it is not random, which is why the word misleads newcomers. Instrumentation noise is usually a step, usually one-directional, and usually concentrated in an identifiable population.

The intellectual lineage runs through three traditions that arrived at the same insight independently. Manufacturing quality control got there first: Shewhart's control charts (1924) separated common-cause from special-cause variation, and the gauge repeatability and reproducibility studies that grew from them made it a rule to qualify the instrument before judging the process, because an unqualified gauge can manufacture a process problem from nothing. Psychometrics got there second, decomposing an observed score into a true score plus error and treating reliability as a property of the instrument, not the subject. Signal detection theory, developed for radar in the 1950s, added that a detection threshold is a choice with asymmetric costs, not a fact. Digital analytics inherited all three in the 2010s, as instrumentation spread across SDKs, app versions, consent regimes and warehouse jobs, each a place where c could change silently. The folk law of the field is Twyman's: any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong. Its best-known operational descendant is the sample ratio mismatch check, which treats a deviation from the intended traffic split as grounds to discard an otherwise beautiful result.

Practitioners who accept the general point nonetheless split into schools that would sign quite different propositions — a disagreement that determines what a team builds, what it monitors, and what it does at 9 a.m. on the morning a number moves.

Kaul's problem is invisible to the instrumentation-first school in its classical form: no event broke, no volume moved, every row landed, and her instrument is a model upgraded deliberately and for good reason. Pandhare's is invisible to the experimentalist school as usually practised, because firmware 2.9 was not an A/B test — except that, as it turned out, it very nearly was.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually do

Begin with the decomposition, which predicts which metrics are fragile. For a ratio R = N/D whose numerator and denominator have capture rates cN and cD, the observed ratio is Robs = Rtrue × (cN/cD). Two consequences are routinely missed. A ratio is invariant to uniform capture loss: lose 30% of everything and a 34% conversion rate still reads 34%. But it is maximally sensitive to differential loss: with a client-instrumented numerator and a server-instrumented denominator, a 30% client-side loss drags 34% to 23.8% with not one user behaving differently. The rule an expert carries is therefore not “check the pipeline” but a question of provenance: do my numerator and denominator share a failure mode? Cross-system ratios lie loudest, and they are disproportionately the metrics executives care about.

The second piece of machinery is an explicit prior, held in numbers rather than temperament. Pandhare's team maintained a change feed — every firmware release, schema change, gateway update and definition edit, timestamped. Over twelve months it recorded 47 changes touching telemetry computation or ingestion, roughly one a week. About one in eight such changes had historically produced a visible artefact: call it six instrument-caused steps a year. Genuine fleet-wide steps of five per cent or more had occurred three times in thirty-six months — monsoon onset, a grid curtailment event, a cyclone — about one a year. The prior odds that a fleet-wide step is instrumental rather than behavioural are therefore roughly six to one, before anyone opens a chart. That number is what justifies spending the first day of an incident on the pipe rather than on the panels, and it is defensible to a CFO in a way that “in my experience it's usually tracking” is not.

Then update it with evidence, using likelihood ratios rather than vibes. Purvai's firmware rollout had been staged by device serial number — effectively at random with respect to geography, installer, panel batch and weather. That detail, decided for operational safety two years earlier, converted the rollout into a natural experiment. The drop was almost entirely confined to systems that had received 2.9: sites on 2.8 held at 4.29 kWh/kWp while 2.9 sites read 3.88. The probability of that confinement given an instrument cause is perhaps 0.8; given weather or soiling, perhaps 0.02, since a randomly assigned firmware cohort has no meteorological identity. A likelihood ratio near 40, applied to prior odds of 6:1, yields posterior odds around 240:1. The arithmetic is crude; the order of magnitude is the point, and writing it down is what stops a room arguing about panels for a week.

The third piece is triangulation, with its one demanding requirement: the second witness must be independent in failure mode, not merely in table name — two dashboards fed by one event stream are one witness. Purvai's genuine second witness was the bi-directional net meter at 412 commercial sites, read monthly on paper by MSEDCL and Torrent Power staff and sharing no code path with the inverter firmware: export down 1.8% year on year. A third, weaker witness, irradiance from a reference weather station, was down 2.1%. The telemetry said 9.5%. The gap is the instrument, and the mechanism was mundane: firmware 2.9 had stopped reading the inverter's monotone lifetime-energy register and begun summing fifteen-minute power samples at the gateway — a sample-and-hold estimator that under-reports badly on the partly-cloudy days of a Gujarat August.

The fourth piece is the one that distinguishes a finished investigation from an abandoned one: reconciliation. It is not enough to find a defect; it must be quantified and the arithmetic closed. Pandhare's analysts modelled the sampling bias against 60 sites with high-frequency logging retained: under-reporting of 7.4% on partly-cloudy days and 0.9% on clear ones, weighting to 6.9% fleet-wide for August. Observed movement 9.5%; instrument 6.9; independently-witnessed real decline about 2; residual 0.6 points, small enough to be soiling and estimation error, and stated rather than assumed away. A team that cannot close its arithmetic to a small residual has not finished; it has merely found something.

4. When the distinction applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be written as testable claims. One: an instrument cause leaves a footprint following a deployment boundary, a behavioural cause a behavioural boundary. Purvai passes emphatically: the move tracks firmware version, not city, season or installer. Kohra fails the test in its usual form, because the judge upgrade hit all traffic at once; with no unaffected population, Kaul's route had to be re-scoring rather than segmentation. Two: a real change propagates proportionally to independently-instrumented correlates. Purvai's correlates barely moved, which is decisive. Kohra's correlate — the share of claims the insurer's own adjudicators accepted unedited, logged in the insurer's system — moved from 68.9% to 70.4%: a gain, but nothing like eleven points. Three: instrument change is discrete in time, behaviour continuous. This is the weakest of the three and misfires most often, because behaviour is discrete whenever the world is: a tariff change, an RBI circular taking effect, a competitor's free tier opening at midnight, the first day of a GST rate change — all produce cliffs with no instrument involved.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. First, when the product change is a measurement change: a consent flow added under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act does not corrupt a metric so much as install a permanent regime in which a knowable fraction of users are genuinely unobservable, and backing it out to restore the old series is a fiction. Second, motivated triage, where “it's probably tracking” becomes an all-purpose solvent for bad news; the tell is that the phrase is only ever used downward. Third, AI-native measurement, where instrument and product are made of the same substance and the dichotomy stops carving at a joint.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the failure is rarely in the team that notices it: a shared event taxonomy lets a platform team's schema migration move a metric owned three floors away, and the change feed that would explain it belongs to neither. The seam, not the code, is the hazard. In two-sided marketplaces, capture is structurally asymmetric — supply-side actions are server-recorded because they touch inventory and money, demand-side actions client-recorded — so any mobile SDK problem presents as a demand collapse, and “buyers have gone quiet while sellers are unchanged” is a claim about instrumentation until proven otherwise. In regulated contexts — Chakravat Payments filing transaction success rates, Vaatavaran Health Systems reporting turnaround times under a diagnostic accreditation regime — the binding constraint is restatement, not diagnosis: a filed number cannot be quietly corrected, re-logging may be prohibited, and the correction travels as an amendment with an audit trail rather than a refreshed dashboard.

Hardware plus software adds two disorienting properties. Rollouts are staged over weeks, so the fleet is a moving mixture of instruments rather than one; and devices buffer, so yesterday's number rewrites itself for days as backlogged records arrive. Purvai's rule — never quote a figure less than 72 hours old — exists because the right edge of every chart is systematically low. AI-native products add a third: the instrument learns. An LLM-as-judge, a labelling rubric, an embedding similarity threshold — each drifts with a version change no data-quality monitor will flag, because volumes, schemas and freshness all look perfect.

How mature companies actually handle the seams, as distinct from how they describe it on stage: one annotated change feed overlaying release, schema, campaign and model-version markers on every dashboard; an analytics on-call rota with authority to hold a number; a metric-freeze window before board reporting; and instrument checks that run whether or not anyone is worried. What they rarely admit is the rest of it — two or three long-tenured analysts who remember which numbers have a second witness and which never did. That tacit inventory is the real asset, and it leaves when they do.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Fixing the instrument creates a second break. The tell is a colleague announcing that history has been backfilled and the series looks clean again. A corrected series contains two discontinuities — the break and the repair — and any trend crossing either is uninterpretable unless the correction is itself versioned. Experts keep explicit definition versions and draw comparisons inside a version, not across a single restated line.

The surviving measured population is a selected sample, not merely a smaller one. The tell is an analyst reassuring the room that the unaffected segment looks fine. When an SDK drops events on battery-constrained devices, the users who remain visible are systematically wealthier, on newer handsets; their retention was always higher. Treating them as a control arm stacks a composition change on the capture change, and the two errors do not cancel.

Definitional drift is more common than pipeline breakage, and invisible to monitoring. The tell is a metric that moved while every event count and freshness check stayed flat. Someone changed a join, an internal-account filter, an attribution window, or the meaning of “active seat” in a pull request no reviewer read as a metrics change. The obvious reading — pipeline healthy, therefore movement real — is exactly backwards.

Absence produces no alert. The tell is an alerting suite composed entirely of thresholds on values. An event that stops firing writes no rows, throws no errors and triggers nothing; the series simply ends, and a chart with fewer points still looks like a chart. Experts monitor the existence and cardinality of series, not just levels, because client events never captured cannot be recovered from any backup.

Triangulation requires independence of failure mode. The tell is a confirming source that shares an upstream job with the source it confirms. Two dashboards, two warehouses and two teams can all be one witness. Trace both estimators back to the sensor and ask what single failure would move both; if one exists, the second number is decoration.

Investigation is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is a bias. The tell is that no one has ever opened an incident ticket for a metric that went up. Organisations litigate bad news and accept good news, which drifts the reported series optimistic over time — a within-company publication bias. The correction is procedural: the same checks fire automatically on any move beyond threshold, in either direction.

Finding a defect is not the same as explaining the movement. The tell is a post-mortem containing a real bug and no arithmetic. Once a plausible culprit surfaces, investigation stops for psychological rather than evidentiary reasons. The expert demand is reconciliation: quantify, subtract, state the residual. A defect explaining one point of a twelve-point move is a finding, not an answer.

A chronic measurement defect becomes a product defect. The tell is a segment “known to under-report” for more than two quarters. Teams optimise what they can see; an under-measured cohort quietly loses its claim on the roadmap, its experiments underpowered and its wins invisible in review. The lens starts shaping the product — Goodhart's law through the back door.

The ability to re-score history is an investment made before you need it. The tell is a team that cannot answer “what would last quarter look like under the new definition?” because the raw inputs were never retained. Kaul could decompose her eleven points only because Kohra had kept every claim document, model output and judge prompt for ninety days. Retaining raw inputs looks like a storage cost until the week it is all that stands between an organisation and an unfalsifiable claim.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the dominant risk is client-side capture: SDKs, OS permission changes, app-version fragmentation across a long tail of Android builds. In B2B and enterprise software it is definitional, because the meaning of usage is renegotiated every time a module, seat type or pricing tier is added; the pipe is robust and the dictionary is not. Platforms and marketplaces inherit both, plus the asymmetry that their two sides are instrumented by different systems. In hardware the instrument is physically distributed, versioned in the field, and reports late. In AI products the instrument is a model whose behaviour changes when it is improved, so the separation between product and measurement becomes a modelling assumption rather than an architectural fact.

Stage changes less than people claim, and where it matters it matters in a specific way. Early-stage companies have one witness for every number and must build the reflex deliberately, since nothing in their environment will catch a defect for them. Large companies have redundant instrumentation almost by accident, and face the opposite problem: numbers that quietly disagree, with nobody owning the reconciliation. What scales with stage is not the technique but the cost of being wrong — the defect that costs a seed-stage team a fortnight costs a listed company a restatement.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Kohra Intelligence: separating the judge from the judged

Kaul refused both shortcuts — reporting the eleven points, and dismissing them. Because Kohra retained raw inputs, she ran a two-by-two: pre-release and post-release traffic, each scored by both judges. The design cost eleven hours of inference and about ₹1.4 lakh in compute.

The decomposition also showed why the new judge scored higher: it handled multi-page discharge summaries competently, and those had been systematically mis-scored as failures before. The old number had been wrong downward for a year — which raised a harder question than the one Kaul started with: whether to restate a year of reported quality upward, under a contract whose quality floor carried commercial consequences.

Purvai Energy Networks: closing the arithmetic

Purvai's reconciliation is set out in Table 3. Its value was not the diagnosis, which took four days, but that every claimant — the Vadodara customer, the channel partners, the lender — received the same closed arithmetic rather than three different reassurances.

Barkha Bazaar: where the discipline itself failed

Barkha Bazaar, a marketplace connecting handloom and home-decor artisans to urban buyers, had trained its analysts well. When GMV per active buyer fell 12% in the fortnight to 18 October 2024, the team opened with the change feed, found a payment-gateway SDK updated four days earlier, and spent sixteen days establishing that it had indeed dropped order-confirmation events for a subset of UPI flows. The defect was real; it accounted for 1.4 percentage points. The team extrapolated the remainder — “likely the same cause, wider than we can measure” — and closed the incident. The other ten points were a seller-side listing-fee experiment ramping from 5% to 40% of sellers over the same fortnight, shifting the catalogue mix toward low-priced items. It ramped for six more weeks. By the time anyone connected the two, Barkha had lost a quarter of roadmap attention while scaling a change that was destroying basket value.

The recovery was procedural. Barkha ruled that no incident could close on a measurement explanation unless the arithmetic reconciled to within two percentage points of the observed movement, residual written into the closing note, and added experiment ramps to the change feed that already carried releases and schema edits. The deeper lesson is uncomfortable for anyone who teaches this topic: a team that has learned to suspect the instrument has acquired a new way to be confidently wrong, because “it was tracking” satisfies as well as any other story and stops inquiry just as effectively.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of late detection

Unreconciled attribution — Barkha's failure. Early warning: a closing note that names a defect but contains no subtraction. Diagnostic: how many of the twelve points does your explanation account for, and what is the residual? Caught late, the true cause keeps ramping and the cost compounds daily.

Motivated triage. Early warning: instrument checks invoked only on downward moves. Diagnostic: would we be investigating if the sign were reversed? Caught late, the series drifts optimistic and the correction lands in front of a board rather than a team.

Restatement without versioning. Early warning: a chart that changed shape retrospectively, with nobody able to say which definition it now uses. Diagnostic: what definition version is each point on this line? Caught late, every analysis crossing the boundary — experiment readouts, cohort comparisons — is quietly wrong.

Monitoring values but not existence. Early warning: alert rules expressed exclusively as thresholds. Diagnostic: which events would page someone if they stopped firing entirely tonight? Caught late, a cohort's behaviour is permanently unrecoverable.

Instrument drift in model-mediated metrics. Early warning: a quality score that moved while traffic, latency and serving configuration were unchanged. Diagnostic: what version of the judge, rubric or labelling guideline produced each number? Caught late, a quarter of model development has been steered by a scoreboard that was itself moving.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does randomisation make triage unnecessary? The experimentalist position at its strongest: instrument error inside a randomised comparison is common to both arms and cancels in the difference, so what needs policing is the split, not the pipe. The evidence is strong: at 412,000 users on an intended 50/50 split, arms of 207,800 and 204,200 give a chi-square near 31 and a p-value around two in a hundred million — a cheap, automatic check that large experimentation programmes credit with catching a meaningful share of invalid results. The position fails where treatments alter logging themselves, which they do whenever a new interface emits new events, and it is silent about the numbers organisations actually fight over: observational trends in board decks.

Restate or version? One camp holds that history should be corrected to the best current understanding, because a series nobody can compare across is useless and an uncorrected number is a known falsehood left standing. The other holds that history should never be rewritten, only annotated and versioned, because restatement destroys the audit trail and creates an incentive to re-restate whenever the current number is inconvenient. Kohra's dilemma — a year of scores now known to be biased downward, under a contract with a quality floor — is exactly the case that separates them. Regulated contexts push toward versioning; investor communication pushes toward restatement.

How much triage is worth buying? The value-of-information school argues that audit effort should be proportional to the decision at stake, and that a culture interrogating every number produces teams that trust nothing and act on nothing. The always-audit school replies that instrument error is not local — a broken metric corrupts every downstream decision, including ones not yet taken — so the expected cost of an unexamined defect far exceeds the incident in front of you. For that to be wrong, instrument defects would have to be mostly self-limiting, which base rates do not support.

Is the dichotomy still coherent? A serious minority argues that in consent-constrained and AI-native products, measurement is part of the product, so “did the product change or the tracking?” presupposes a separation that no longer exists. The counter-argument is operational rather than philosophical: the question still routes work — to engineering or to the data platform — and no alternative framing has produced a better first question at nine in the morning. Neither side has conceded.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether tracking changed, once, early, and is satisfied by an answer. Someone who has internalised it differs in four visible ways. They hold a written prior about their own environment, updated from the change feed, so their first estimate is a number rather than a mood. They know without looking which metrics have a second witness with an independent failure mode and which have none, and treat the second group as provisional even when nothing appears wrong. They build the capability to re-score history before an incident requires it, because retained raw inputs and versioned definitions are the only tools that work when there is no unaffected population to segment. And they close the arithmetic: a residual, stated aloud, is the difference between an investigation and a story.

They also speak differently in a room: ranges rather than points when the instrument is uncertain, comfort in saying a number cannot bear the weight being placed on it, and the same scrutiny applied to metrics that moved in their favour. Above all they treat measurement as a product with its own roadmap, defects and users, rather than as plumbing that either works or does not.

12. What each of them decided

Kaul went to the 19 August review with the two-by-two, not the eleven points. Kohra reported a product improvement of 2.4 percentage points with stated uncertainty, disclosed the judge upgrade as a metric-definition change, and published the series in two versioned tracks rather than one restated line. On the contractual floor she recommended the harder path: telling the insurer the historical series had been biased low, offering the re-scored history and a jointly supervised 600-claim audit as arbiter, and declining to claim the floor was met until it returned. Nambiar accepted, reluctantly, reasoning that a renewal won on a number his own analytics chief could not defend would surface as a liability at the worst moment.

Pandhare made the symmetrical call. Purvai reverted the daily-energy computation to the inverter's cumulative register in firmware 2.9.1, kept the fifteen-minute samples as an operational diagnostic rather than a billing input, and moved channel-partner payouts off telemetry entirely onto utility net-meter readings, accepting a monthly cadence in exchange for a witness the company does not control. The Vadodara SLA claim was answered with the reconciliation table and declined; the real two per cent decline was disclosed to the lender in the same pack, alongside the irradiance data, on the view that a company which corrects its own numbers downward once buys more credibility than it spends.

Discussion questions.

  1. Kohra's old quality number was biased downward for a year. Does the company owe its insurer a restatement, a versioned disclosure, or nothing at all — and would your answer change if the bias had run the other way?
  2. Purvai's staged-by-serial-number rollout turned a firmware release into a natural experiment, by accident. What would it cost each of these companies to make that property deliberate for every change that touches measurement, and who should own the decision?
  3. Barkha Bazaar's analysts did everything the textbook asks and still lost a quarter. What rule, stated in a sentence, would have caught it — and what does that rule cost on the many occasions when the measurement explanation is in fact the whole story?

13. Going deeper

  • Root cause analysis of a metric change — begins where this one ends; worth doing only once the movement survives the instrument check, and it inherits the residual as its brief.
  • Anomaly detection and alerting — turns this judgement into a system, and forces the questions about thresholds, seasonality and the false-positive cost that erodes trust in alerts.
  • Constructing a funnel — the archetype of cross-system ratios, with steps instrumented by different teams; building one properly is where provenance discipline is learned.
  • Reading drop-off — distinguishing a step where users leave from a step where the event simply does not fire is this topic applied at the sharpest resolution.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — a definition before it is a behaviour, which makes it the metric most exposed to semantic drift and the most valuable to version.
  • Cohort analysis — the natural home of the versioned series: cohorts let you compare like with like across a definition or instrument boundary rather than through it.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the shape capture loss most easily counterfeits; reading curves well means knowing which part of the curve your instrument can see.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — ratios of activity over windows, exquisitely sensitive to differential capture between numerator and denominator; a good test of whether this arithmetic has landed.

Pratyaksh AI: Three Numbers and a Cure Period

An AI document-intelligence company has one accuracy figure from its own laboratory, a different one from its largest client's auditors, and a third from a client who changed how documents arrive. The cure period expires in eleven days.

1. Sunday night, 22 February 2026 — Indiranagar, Bengaluru

Ritwik Sanyal had three windows open and did not trust any of them. On the left was Pratyaksh AI's own evaluation dashboard, which said that Darpan v4 extracted fields from lending documents at 99.1 per cent accuracy, up from 97.9 per cent for the model it replaced. In the middle was a PDF that had arrived on Friday evening from the internal audit team at Mawrid Finance in Dubai, Pratyaksh's largest customer, which said that over 900 sampled files the same product had achieved 96.4 per cent — below the 98.5 per cent floor written into a contract worth ₹14.2 crore a year. On the right was a Slack thread in which the delivery lead for Vindhya Credit in Hyderabad reported that the share of loan files completing without human review had fallen from about three-quarters to two-thirds since the first week of January, and that the operations head there had begun asking uncomfortable questions in weekly reviews.

The contractual cure period ran to Friday, 6 March. Pratyaksh's board met on Thursday, 26 February. Devika Menon, the co-founder and chief executive, had asked Ritwik for a recommendation by close of business on Monday, in one page, with a number in it.

What bothered him was not that the three numbers disagreed. It was that he could not say, at eleven o'clock on a Sunday night, what any one of them was a measurement of.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Pratyaksh AI was founded in Bengaluru in 2021 by Devika Menon and Ayesha Qureshi, who had met building fraud models at a payments company. Its product, Darpan, read the documents that Indian lending runs on — salary slips, bank statements, GST returns, Udyam registrations, Aadhaar-masked KYC packets, property papers — and turned them into structured fields with a confidence score against each. Lenders used it to decide which files could move straight through to underwriting and which needed a human. The commercial promise was simple: every percentage point of straight-through processing removed cost from a loan file, and every extraction error that reached underwriting put a lender at regulatory risk.

By February 2026 Pratyaksh had fourteen paying clients and about ₹39.7 crore of annual recurring revenue. It sat in a crowded and fast-professionalising Indian market, where lenders had learned from the last decade to ask hard questions: a generation of founders who had watched Razorpay, Zerodha and Groww build infrastructure-grade trust now expected vendors to substantiate claims the way Zoho and Freshworks had taught enterprise buyers to expect. Pratyaksh's differentiation was not the model. It was that its numbers had, historically, held up under audit.

The decision that constrained everything in February had been taken in October 2023. Mawrid Finance, a mid-sized lender headquartered in the Dubai International Financial Centre with an Indian-expatriate retail book, had been willing to sign a three-year contract on one condition: Darpan had to run inside Mawrid's own data centre, because Mawrid's compliance committee would not permit customer documents to leave the jurisdiction. Pratyaksh was eighteen months old and the contract was larger than its entire book. It said yes.

The consequence was a second lineage. The cloud product shipped weekly, emitted full event-level telemetry into Pratyaksh's warehouse, and could be re-analysed at any time. The on-premise product shipped quarterly as a signed appliance image, ran on whatever hardware the client had, and returned only a weekly aggregate file — counts and rates, no raw events — because anything richer would have required a data-transfer approval that Mawrid's committee had declined twice. In 2023 that had looked like a commercial concession. By 2026 it meant that the company could not, even in principle, recompute a historical number for its largest customer.

3. The industry around it

Indian lending in 2026 was a regulated, instrumented, and impatient business. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework had pushed lenders to document their underwriting chain end to end; the account aggregator network had made consented financial data routine; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made every transfer of customer documents a question for a legal team rather than an engineer. GST filing formats had been revised in the previous financial year and Udyam certificates had changed layout in September 2025, which meant that a document type Darpan had read reliably for two years now arrived in two visually different forms.

Competitive pressure came from two directions. Large system integrators — the Infosys and TCS practices that already sat inside every large bank — offered document extraction as part of a wider transformation programme and were happy to price it near zero. At the other end, a handful of well-funded Indian API companies sold extraction by the call. Pratyaksh survived in the middle by selling an outcome rather than a model: a contractual straight-through-processing rate and a contractual accuracy floor, with service credits attached to both. That was a good commercial position for as long as the company could measure itself credibly, and an extremely exposed one the moment it could not.

4. What happened, in order

October 2025. To scale annotation, Pratyaksh moved ground-truth labelling from a six-person in-house team in Bengaluru to a specialist vendor with a floor in Coimbatore. The vendor's rubric, agreed in a one-hour call, introduced semantic equivalence: a date rendered 05-04-2025 where the document said 5 April 2025 would now be scored correct, as would a name captured as "Sunil Kumar R" where the document read "R. Sunil Kumar". Under the old in-house rubric both were errors. Nobody recorded the change as a metric-definition change, because nobody thought of the rubric as part of the metric.

November 2025. The evaluation set was refreshed. The old golden set of 4,000 fields, assembled in June 2024, had drifted away from the document mix Pratyaksh actually saw; a new set of 6,500 fields was sampled from recent production volume and labelled by the new vendor under the new rubric. The refresh was documented in an engineering note and celebrated as overdue hygiene.

18 December 2025. Darpan v4.0 shipped to cloud clients. It carried a new extraction model, and it also lowered the auto-accept confidence threshold from 0.86 to 0.79 — a change Ayesha's team justified on the evidence that the new model's confidence scores were better calibrated, and that Sales had been asking for a higher straight-through rate for a year. The release note described the model. The threshold change appeared in a configuration diff.

7 January 2026. The v4.1 on-premise appliance image was cut for Mawrid. Because Mawrid's servers carried an older generation of GPU, Karthik Subramanian's field team produced an int8-quantised build so that latency would stay inside the contracted 3.5 seconds per file. The quantised build passed a smoke test of 120 files. It was never run against the evaluation set, because the evaluation harness lived in Pratyaksh's cloud and the quantised weights had been compiled for hardware Pratyaksh did not own.

Same release. The v4.1 agent changed what counted as a human touch. Under the old agent, a reviewer opening a file counted the file as touched, and therefore not straight-through. Under the new agent, only an edit or a rejection counted. The change had been requested by a client who complained that supervisors spot-checking files were depressing their own numbers. It shipped in both cloud and on-premise builds.

5 January 2026. Vindhya Credit launched a new sourcing channel in which field agents photographed documents on handsets in borrowers' homes, rather than collecting them as branch-scanned PDFs.

13 February 2026. Mawrid's internal audit delivered its quarterly sample. Accuracy: 96.4 per cent. Straight-through processing: 79.2 per cent, comfortably above the contracted 72. One number was a breach; the other was the best the account had ever recorded.

5. The people

Ritwik Sanyal, VP Product, Bengaluru. Three years at Pratyaksh. He owns the recommendation and the accuracy claim on the website. His position is that the company should not defend a number it cannot reproduce. What he is not saying is that he approved the threshold change in December on a one-line Slack message without reading the calibration analysis, and that he has not told Devika this.

Devika Menon, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. She is mid-way through a bridge round and has told two prospective investors that Darpan v4 lifted accuracy above 99 per cent. Her stated position is that the company must be scrupulous with clients. Her incentive is a term sheet due in April. What she is not saying is that she has already been asked, by the lead investor's diligence team, for the evaluation methodology, and has not yet replied.

Ayesha Qureshi, co-founder and Head of ML, Pune. She believes the model is genuinely better and says so with evidence: on any fixed set, under any single rubric, v4 beats v3. Her incentive is that v4 is the work of eleven months and four crore rupees of compute. What she is not saying is that she argued against the quantised build in December, lost the argument to latency, and has no benchmark of her own for the weights actually running in Dubai.

Karthik Subramanian, Head of Field Engineering, Chennai. He owns the nine engineers who deploy and maintain on-premise appliances. His position is that on-premise clients cannot be treated as second-class and that the company should stop pretending cloud metrics generalise. His incentive is headcount: he has been asking for four more engineers for two quarters. What he is not saying is that his team's smoke test of the quantised build covered only clean scanned PDFs, and that he knows it.

Sandeep Bhatia, SVP Sales, New Jersey. He carries the Gulf and North American number and has a ₹9 crore pipeline that cites the 99.1 per cent figure in three proposals. His position is that the Mawrid audit is methodologically unfair — it counts a transposed initial as an error — and that Pratyaksh should contest it. His incentive is an accelerator on new bookings. What he is not saying is that Mawrid's head of operations has already asked him, informally, what the renewal would look like at a lower price.

Priyanka Raut, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. She has spent the last ten days doing the only clean work in the case: reconstructing what each number measures. Her position is that none of the three figures are comparable and that the company should say so plainly. Her incentive is intellectual and reputational; she joined from a firm where she had watched exactly this failure. What she is not saying is that she flagged the golden-set refresh as a comparability risk in a November document that nobody read, and that she is quietly angry about it.

Wei Lin Ong, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. She covers Mawrid and the two South-East Asian accounts and has been on calls at 8 am Gulf time for three weeks. Her position is that Mawrid's trust is the asset at risk, not the SLA credit. Her incentive is net revenue retention. What she is not saying is that Mawrid's audit team asked her in January whether the Dubai deployment ran the same model as the cloud, and that she said yes, believing it.

Johanna Krebs, Design and Research Lead, Berlin. She has watched fourteen hours of reviewer sessions at Amba Housing Finance in Mumbai. Her position is that the straight-through number has become meaningless because reviewers behave differently when they know it is measured: since January, supervisors at two clients have been opening files in a read-only mode precisely because it no longer counts. Her incentive is to get research taken seriously in a company run by engineers. What she is not saying is that she has no idea how widespread the behaviour is.

He asked whether the Dubai deployment runs the same software as the Indian ones. I said I would come back to him."

8. The options, as Ritwik currently sees them

Option A — Contest the audit. Ask Mawrid for its 900-file sample list, re-score under a jointly agreed rubric, and argue the breach away. Upside: cheap, fast, and probably right on the narrow question of name and date formatting. Cost: it spends the relationship's goodwill on a technicality, and if the re-score still lands below 98.5 — which the quantisation question makes entirely possible — Pratyaksh has conceded the argument and lost eleven days.

Option B — Restore the confidence threshold to 0.86 across all deployments. Upside: by Exhibit 5 it lifts the accuracy of the auto-accepted population by about 0.8 points immediately, which may be enough to clear the floor. Cost: it cuts the straight-through rate by roughly eleven points, which would put Mawrid at about 68 per cent against a contracted 72, converting an accuracy breach into a throughput breach; and it would reverse the single change most cited in Sandeep's live pipeline.

Option C — Roll the on-premise appliance back to v3.2 and tell Mawrid why. Upside: it returns Mawrid to a build with a two-year audit history and removes the unbenchmarked quantisation from the field. Cost: nine field engineers, an estimated six weeks, ₹1.1 crore of unplanned delivery cost, and a disclosure that Pratyaksh shipped weights to its largest client that it had never evaluated — a sentence that will not stay inside the account.

Each of the three assumes that one of the numbers is the true one and the others are wrong. None of them asks what would have to be measured, and on what population, for the question to have an answer at all. Priyanka has said as much twice; Ritwik has not yet worked out whether she is being rigorous or merely unhelpful eleven days before a deadline.

9. Deadlines and hard constraints

The cure period ends Friday, 6 March. Unremedied, the accuracy breach triggers service credits of ₹3.4 crore against a ₹14.2 crore contract and gives Mawrid a termination right at the anniversary in December. The board meets on Thursday, 26 February; the bridge round's lead investor has an outstanding diligence question about evaluation methodology that Devika has not answered. Amba's renewal falls on 31 March and Amba's procurement team has asked, routinely, for Pratyaksh's latest published accuracy figure.

The binding constraints are not financial. Mawrid's files cannot leave Dubai; the DPDP Act and the client's own DIFC undertaking both bite, and the compliance committee meets fortnightly, next on 4 March. Pratyaksh owns no hardware of the generation on which the quantised build runs. The v3 serving stack needs four engineering days to restore, and Ayesha's team of nine is also carrying the v4.2 release promised to three cloud clients in March. There is ₹46 crore of cash against ₹2.7 crore of monthly burn, which is comfortable enough that money is not the constraint and uncomfortable enough that a ₹3.4 crore credit and a delayed round together would change the company's plan for the year.

10. Questions for discussion

1. List every change between October 2025 and February 2026 that could move a reported accuracy or straight-through number. For each, say whether it changed the product, the population, or the measurement — and note the ones where you cannot tell from the case.

2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 disagree. For each pair, state precisely what would have to be true for both to be correct simultaneously.

3. Exhibit 5 shows accuracy and straight-through processing being computed over populations whose boundary the company itself moved in December. What does that imply about the two SLAs as a contractual instrument, and what should Pratyaksh have negotiated instead in 2023?

4. Johanna's observation about reviewers opening files in preview is based on four people. How much weight should it carry, and what is the cheapest way to find out whether it generalises before 6 March?

5. Six of the eight stakeholders are withholding something. Which omission is most consequential for the decision, and how should a product leader surface it without turning the week into an inquest?

6. What should Ritwik do on Monday morning, in what order, and what exactly should he say to the board on Thursday about a company whose headline product claim rests on a comparison it can no longer reproduce?

Midnight, and a blank page

At a quarter past midnight Ritwik closed the audit PDF and opened a blank page for the one-pager Devika had asked for. He typed a heading — What we know — and then sat looking at it. Under it he could write that v4 beat v3 on Set B, which was true and which Ayesha would defend. He could write that Mawrid's auditors found 96.4 per cent, which was also true. He could write that the two sentences had almost nothing to do with each other, which was the only honest thing on the page and the one sentence that could not be said to a board in a bridge round.

Outside, on 100 Feet Road, the last of the Sunday traffic had thinned. He thought about Wei Lin's note, and about Hamdan Al-Saadi's question — whether the Dubai deployment ran the same software as the Indian ones — and about the fact that the truthful answer was not exactly, and we do not know how much that matters. He deleted the heading and typed a different one: What we would need to measure to know anything. Then he looked at the calendar, counted eleven days, and deleted that too.

Mithila Bazaar: The Number Before Diwali

A social-commerce platform watches its core conversion metric fall six points in the fortnight before its biggest selling season. Roll back, cut spend, or find out what actually moved?

1. Wednesday, 8 October 2025 — Koramangala, Bengaluru

Sharanya Kulkarni had been at her desk since half past six, which at Mithila Bazaar in October was not unusual, and had spent the first ninety minutes of it looking at a single line on a single chart. The line was reseller order completion: of every hundred catalogues a reseller shared into a WhatsApp group, how many produced at least one placed order within seventy-two hours. It was the number the company reported to its board, the number on which the growth team's quarterly targets rested, and the number the head of growth had put into the Diwali marketing plan.

For most of the year the line had sat at 27 to 28 per cent. In the week beginning 29 September it printed 24.9. In the week beginning 6 October it printed 21.3. Diwali fell on 20 October. Mithila Bazaar's investor update was due on Wednesday, 15 October, and the finance team needed a decision on the ₹6 crore of festival performance marketing — roughly forty per cent of the quarter's entire acquisition budget — by Friday the 10th, because the media buys had to be confirmed with the platforms before the weekend.

Three people had already told Sharanya what to do, and each of them had told her something different.

2. The company

Mithila Bazaar, founded in Bengaluru in 2019, ran a reseller marketplace for apparel, kitchenware and home furnishing. Its users were not shoppers but sellers: about 4.2 lakh monthly active resellers, three-quarters of them women in tier-two and tier-three towns from Muzaffarpur to Belagavi, who browsed the catalogue in the app, forwarded product cards into WhatsApp groups of neighbours and relatives, collected orders, and took a margin they set themselves. Mithila Bazaar handled sourcing from suppliers in Surat, Tiruppur and Panipat, logistics, payments over UPI, and returns.

The model was not novel — Meesho had built it at far greater scale, and Flipkart and Amazon both ran reseller programmes — but Mithila Bazaar had found a defensible position in heavier, higher-value home categories where per-order margins supported the cost of assisted delivery. Gross merchandise value in the September quarter was ₹210 crore, average order value ₹740, and the take rate a little under eleven per cent. The company had raised a Series B in 2024 and expected to raise again in the middle of 2026; the Diwali quarter was, in every sense, the quarter that would be shown to those investors.

The team had grown up global in the way Indian product companies now do. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune; Lukas Brandt, who led design, worked from Berlin and had spent August redesigning the share sheet — the screen from which a reseller pushed a catalogue into WhatsApp — after watching twenty session recordings in which resellers had given up on it. Nandita Rao, the company's only senior data scientist, worked from Toronto and joined stand-ups at what was, for her, a civilised 10 pm. Mei Lin Tan ran customer success from Singapore for the small but growing set of resellers serving the Indian diaspora in South-East Asia and the Gulf.

3. What happened

On 28 September, Mithila Bazaar shipped Android build 5.2. It contained three things. Lukas's redesigned share sheet was one. The second was a consent screen, built to satisfy the company's reading of its obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which asked resellers to confirm processing preferences on first launch. The third was invisible to users: the app moved off a third-party analytics SDK and onto Mithila Bazaar's own first-party event pipeline, a migration the data team had wanted for eighteen months, both to control cost and to reduce the amount of reseller data leaving the company's own systems.

The iOS build containing the same three changes had been submitted on 26 September and was still, on 8 October, awaiting review. Android build 5.2 had gone to thirty per cent of users in the week of 29 September and to eighty-five per cent in the week of 6 October. About nine per cent of Mithila Bazaar's resellers used iPhones; the rest were on Android, and around a sixth of those had automatic updates disabled and were still on 5.1 or older.

Arjun Dua, the head of growth in Gurugram, had drawn the obvious conclusion on the evening of 6 October and written it in the leadership channel: the share sheet redesign had broken the flow, resellers were sharing but not converting, and the build should be rolled back before the festival. He had a plausible mechanism — the new sheet moved the price-setting control below the fold — and he had the chart.

Praveen Gowda, the engineering manager in Pune, was less sure. He pointed out that the fall had begun in the same week as the SDK migration and that the new pipeline had been live for exactly as long as the new share sheet, since both rode build 5.2. Nandita Rao, awake in Toronto and reading the thread at what was late evening for her, asked a question that neither of them had asked: what did the settlement ledger say?

4. The people

Sharanya Kulkarni, Director of Product, Bengaluru. Two years at Mithila Bazaar, eight before that across Razorpay-adjacent fintech and a consumer app. She owned the metric, the release train and the recommendation that would go to the board on 15 October. Her instinct was that a six-point fall arriving in a single step, in one fortnight, in a metric that had been stable for eleven months, was too tidy to be human behaviour.

Arjun Dua, Head of Growth, Gurugram. Compensated on activated resellers and on festival GMV. He wanted the rollback because the downside of rolling back a redesign was three sprint-weeks and the downside of a broken festival was his year. He had also, privately, never liked the share sheet redesign.

Nandita Rao, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. She had owned the SDK migration jointly with Praveen and would be the person blamed if it had gone wrong, which made her caution in the thread notable. She had access to two independent counts of orders: the one the app reported, and the one the payments and settlement system produced for reconciliation with the company's payment aggregator.

Praveen Gowda, Engineering Manager, Pune. Responsible for build 5.2. He could roll the share sheet back by configuration flag in about four hours without a new app-store release, but rolling back the event pipeline would take a full build, review and staged rollout — at least six days, taking the company past Diwali.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Weekly catalogue shares and orders, all platforms (figures in lakh, except rates)

Source: Mithila Bazaar product analytics (columns 2–4) and the payments reconciliation extract prepared weekly by the finance team for the company's payment aggregator (column 5). The two systems share no code. The settlement ledger counts an order when payment is authorised or a cash-on-delivery order is confirmed by the logistics partner; it has historically run within 0.5 per cent of the app-tracked count.

Exhibit 1 is the document that should stop an argument. Until the week of 29 September the two order counts agree to within a rounding error, as they always had. From that week they diverge, and they diverge in opposite directions: the app-tracked count falls from 11.68 lakh to 10.46 lakh while the settlement ledger rises from 11.71 lakh to 13.28 lakh. Catalogue shares — the denominator — rose in both weeks, which is what one would expect in the run-up to Diwali. If the settlement ledger is right, resellers placed more orders in the week of 6 October than in any week of the quarter.
