Exhibit 3 narrows the question but does not close it. Both segments that did not receive build 5.2 are unchanged at about 28 per cent, and the whole of the fall sits in the segment that did. That rules out a general market effect, a seasonal effect and a competitor effect — none of which would politely confine themselves to one Android build. It does not, on its own, separate Arjun's explanation from Praveen's, because build 5.2 changed the share sheet and the measurement of the share sheet in the same artefact.

What separates them is Exhibit 1. A broken share sheet reduces orders. It cannot increase them. The settlement ledger, which is produced by a different system for a different purpose and is reconciled to money actually moving over UPI, says orders rose 13.4 per cent in the two weeks after the build. The only explanation consistent with both exhibits is that resellers on build 5.2 are placing more orders than before and the app is recording fewer of them.

6. The options

Option A — Roll back the share sheet on Thursday. Praveen can disable the redesign by flag in four hours, restoring the 5.1 experience to every Android user. Upside: if Arjun is right, the festival is saved with six days to spare and the cost is three sprint-weeks of Lukas's work. Cost: the rollback does not touch the event pipeline, so if the pipeline is the cause the metric will not recover, the team will have burned the week, and a redesign that early session recordings suggested was a genuine improvement will be reversed on no evidence. It also tells the organisation that a chart is enough to reverse a design decision.

Option B — Cut the festival spend from ₹6 crore to ₹3.5 crore and reset the board's expectations on 15 October. Upside: if completion really has fallen to 21 per cent, every rupee of acquisition is now buying twenty-three per cent less GMV, and cutting protects roughly ₹2.5 crore of cash going into a fundraising year. Cost: if the fall is an artefact, Mithila Bazaar forfeits its highest-return fortnight of the year — at the settlement-ledger run rate, roughly ₹19 crore of festival GMV and about ₹2.1 crore of take — and enters investor conversations having told a story about a conversion collapse that did not happen.

Option C — Freeze both spend and rollback for forty-eight hours; reconcile the app-tracked count against the settlement ledger at the level of individual orders; ship an instrumentation fix rather than a product rollback. Upside: it is the only option that resolves the ambiguity rather than betting on one side of it, and reconciliation at order level either finds the missing events or does not, within two days. Cost: Friday's media deadline passes without a confirmed buy, which costs rate and inventory in the most competitive fortnight of the Indian retail calendar; and if the reconciliation is inconclusive, Sharanya arrives at Monday with less time and no more certainty.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What exactly does Exhibit 1 establish that Exhibit 3 does not? State the claim in one sentence, and say what would have to be true of the settlement ledger for that claim to fail.

2. Build 5.2 shipped a product change and a measurement change together. What did that decision cost Mithila Bazaar in this fortnight, and what would a policy of separating them have cost the team over the preceding year?

3. Arjun, Praveen and Nandita each have an incentive that points at a different explanation. How should Sharanya use that fact when weighing their arguments, without treating anyone as arguing in bad faith?

4. Which option should Sharanya take on Thursday, 9 October, and what precisely will she say to the board on the 15th about a metric she has just discovered was wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the first question of any metric investigation: did the product change, or did the tracking? Almost every instinct in a company under time pressure is to skip it. A chart moves, someone proposes a mechanism, and the organisation begins debating the mechanism rather than the chart. Arjun's story about the price control below the fold is a good story. It is also untested, and the debate it started consumed two days before anyone asked whether the fall was real.

A well-reasoned answer here rests on a discipline rather than a hunch: find a count of the same thing that does not pass through the same pipeline. Mithila Bazaar had one, and had it for an unglamorous reason — the finance team reconciled orders to the payment aggregator every week. That ledger is the single most valuable artefact in the case, because a broken product and a broken pipeline look identical in the app's own data and completely different once a second, independent count is laid beside it. The shape of the evidence matters too: the fall is a clean step aligned to a build, confined entirely to the population that received that build, and present in a segment cut where behaviour and instrumentation changed together — all classic marks of an instrumentation break rather than a behaviour change.

One defensible path is Option C, executed narrowly. Sharanya holds the rollback, because rolling back the share sheet tests nothing and destroys a design decision; she confirms the festival media buy at the planned ₹6 crore, because the settlement ledger — the count tied to money — says demand is not merely intact but rising; and she gives Nandita and Praveen forty-eight hours to reconcile order IDs between the two systems. The likely finding, given that the consent screen and the new pipeline shipped together, is that a share of build-5.2 sessions is producing orders whose events carry no usable identifier, so the join from share to order fails and the order is never attributed to the catalogue that produced it. That is a fix in the pipeline, not in the product.

What she says to the board on 15 October matters as much as what she does on the 9th. The honest report is not "the metric was wrong"; it is that the company published for two weeks a number whose collection had changed underneath it, that a second independent count existed and was not consulted for eight days, and that from this quarter every headline metric will be published beside the settlement-ledger equivalent, with the gap shown. The instrumentation bug will be fixed within the week. The habit of shipping product and measurement in the same release, and of reading one number without its independent twin, is the thing that will otherwise recur next Diwali.
